🌱 For young readers

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.

About 2,080 years ago, a Roman poet named Lucretius wrote a long poem with a big idea: everything in the world is made of tiny bits, far too small to see, that are always moving. He called them the "first-beginnings" of things. We call them atoms.

How could he know about things nobody could see? He used clues. Wet clothes dry in the sun, but you never see the water leave. A stone step wears down over many years, but you never see a single bit go. So, he said, the bits must be too small to see.

blocks.name: gb-atoms
blocks.cap: Watch the black speck get knocked about by tiny moving bodies. Then hide them: the speck still wanders.

blocks.html:
🧩 Try this

A smell race. Have someone open a jar of something with a strong smell, like an orange peel or vanilla, at one end of a room. Stand at the other end and time how long until you smell it. Nothing visible crossed the room. What did? Lucretius would say: tiny bodies, moving through the air.

Lucretius also noticed dust dancing in a sunbeam in a dark room, and thought invisible bodies were knocking it about. Today we know the dust is mostly pushed by moving air, but very tiny specks seen under a microscope really are jiggled by bumping molecules. That jiggling helped prove atoms exist, about 1,950 years after Lucretius wrote.

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Titus Lucretius Carus (c. 99–c. 55 BC) lived in the last years of the Roman Republic, a time of civil wars. Almost nothing is known of his life. His one work, On the Nature of Things (De rerum natura), is a poem in six books. The orator Cicero mentions it in a letter of 54 BC, praising both its brilliance and its skill.

Lucretius followed the Greek philosopher Epicurus (341–270 BC), who taught that the aim of life is peace of mind, and that the greatest threats to it are fear of the gods and fear of death. Lucretius's problem was how to free his readers from those fears. His answer was physics: if people understood that everything happens by natural causes, he argued, they would stop being afraid. These are Lucretius's own views about religion and death; readers, religious and not, have long argued with them.

Lucretius's two first principles: nothing comes from nothing, and nothing is ever destroyed into nothing. Everything is made of atoms, which can't be created or destroyed, moving in empty space (the void).

blocks.text: Evidence for bodies you can't see

blocks.html: This is a good argument from evidence: we see the total loss, so something must be leaving, but each piece is too small to see. It still works. A gold ring worn every day for fifty years loses a measurable amount of gold, a few atoms at a time.

blocks.title: How small?
blocks.q: Suppose a gold ring loses 0.06 grams over 30 years of wear. A gram of gold has about $3 \times 10^{21}$ atoms. About how many atoms leave each second?
steps: Atoms lost: $0.06 \times 3 \times 10^{21} = 1.8 \times 10^{20}$.
Seconds in 30 years: $30 \times 365 \times 24 \times 3600 \approx 9.5 \times 10^{8}$.
Per second: $1.8 \times 10^{20} \div 9.5 \times 10^{8} \approx 1.9 \times 10^{11}$, about 200 billion atoms every second, and still you can't see the ring change from day to day.

blocks.name: gb-atoms
blocks.cap: A large speck among many small moving bodies. Hide the small ones and watch the speck wander.

blocks.html: Saying Lucretius discovered Brownian motion. The dust in a sunbeam is moved mostly by air currents, not by single molecules; it is far too big. The real effect was seen by the botanist Robert Brown in 1827, watching pollen grains' tiny particles under a microscope. Einstein explained it mathematically in 1905, and Jean Perrin's measurements of 1908 convinced nearly all scientists that atoms are real. Lucretius had the right idea for the wrong example.

blocks.title: A random walk
blocks.q: A speck is knocked one tiny step in a random direction each time. On average, how far from its start is it after 100 steps of 1 micrometer? After 400?
steps: For a random walk, the typical distance grows as the square root of the number of steps.
After 100 steps: $\sqrt{100} \times 1 = 10$ micrometers.
After 400 steps: $\sqrt{400} \times 1 = 20$ micrometers. Four times the steps, only twice the distance.

items: Book II: atoms come in many shapes but not infinitely many; they fall through the void and sometimes "swerve" slightly, which Lucretius uses to explain free will.
Book III: the mind and spirit are made of very fine atoms and do not survive death, so death, he argues, is nothing to fear.
Book IV: how we see, hear and dream.
Book V: how the world, life and human society began, including an early picture of living things that failed to survive because they were not fitted to their surroundings.
Book VI: thunder, earthquakes, volcanoes, magnets and disease.

blocks.text: What later science kept, and what it changed

items: Kept: conservation (Lavoisier, 1789, showed that mass is neither created nor destroyed in chemical change); atoms (Dalton, 1808); and the habit of explaining the visible by the invisible.
Changed: atoms are not indivisible. The electron was found in 1897 and the nucleus in 1911. And they are not tiny hooked or smooth pellets, as Lucretius pictured.

Wrong: following Epicurus, Lucretius said the Sun is about as big as it looks, and he rejected the idea that things fall toward a center, which led him to deny that people could live on the other side of a round Earth.

blocks.html:
🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

By the Middle Ages the poem had nearly vanished. In 1417 the Italian book hunter Poggio Bracciolini found a copy in a German monastery and had it copied. Printed in 1473, it was read by Montaigne (later on this ladder), who quotes it often; by the philosopher Pierre Gassendi, who revived atomism in the 1600s; and by Thomas Jefferson, who owned several copies. Scientists of the 1600s such as Boyle and Newton built on an atomism that owed much to Epicurus and Lucretius, though they put it within a world made by God.

Some recent writers have claimed that this one rediscovery started the modern world. Many historians think that goes too far: the scientific revolution had many causes. But the poem was one of the routes by which ancient atomism reached early modern science.

Lucretius believed that understanding nature brings calm. Many readers since have shared some version of that hope; others have argued that his picture of a purposeless world leaves something out. Dante, Milton and Pascal, later on this ladder, offer very different accounts. The question of what science can and cannot tell us about how to live is one the Great Books keep returning to.

items: Is it reasonable to believe in things nobody can see? What evidence would convince you?
Lucretius thought knowing the causes of things would take away fear. Does understanding something make it less frightening?
A poem taught science for centuries. Can poetry teach science well?

blocks.html:
💬 Talk about it together

  1. Do the smell race. How else could you show that tiny invisible things are moving around you?
  2. Lucretius said nothing comes from nothing. Can you think of anything that seems to come from nothing? Where does it really come from?
  3. When a log burns, it seems to disappear. Where does it go?
  4. Why do you think Lucretius wrote about science as a poem instead of a plain book?
  5. Lucretius was right about atoms but for some wrong reasons. Is it still fair to give him credit?

🌱 For young readers

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.

Before he wrote his great story of Aeneas, the Roman poet Virgil wrote about the countryside where he grew up. His first poems, the Eclogues, are songs sung by shepherds as they watch their flocks. His next poem, the Georgics, is about farming: how to plow, when to plant, how to grow grapes and olives, how to care for cows and horses, and how to keep bees.
Virgil loved the country, but he knew farming was hard work. He tells farmers to watch the sky and the animals for signs of the weather, and to do each job at the right time of year.

🧩 Try this

Be a weather watcher. For one week, write down the weather each morning and one thing you notice outdoors: the clouds, the wind, how birds fly, how the air smells. Each evening, guess tomorrow’s weather from your signs, then check. Which of your signs worked best? Real forecasters today use instruments and computers, but they began by watching carefully, just as Virgil told farmers to do.

blocks.name: gb-georgics
blocks.cap: Tap a book of the Georgics to see what it is about, or switch to the ten Eclogues.

blocks.html: In the last book Virgil writes about bees as if a hive were a tiny city, where everyone has a job and all the work is shared.

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Virgil (70–19 BC) came from farm country near Mantua, in northern Italy. The Eclogues, ten short poems published around 39 BC, were his first book. The Georgics, a poem of four books on farming, took him about seven years and was finished around 29 BC. Both were written as Rome came out of civil war, when Octavian (soon to be called Augustus) was taking power. Virgil’s friend and patron Maecenas, a close adviser of Octavian, is named at the start of every book of the Georgics.

The Eclogues follow the Greek poet Theocritus, whose shepherds sang in the hills of Sicily. Virgil’s herdsmen hold singing contests, mourn a lost friend and sing of love. But Roman troubles break in. After the civil war battle of Philippi in 42 BC, farmland in northern Italy was taken to settle veteran soldiers. The first Eclogue opens with two herdsmen: one has been driven from his land, the other allowed to stay.

The fourth Eclogue is the most famous. It foretells the birth of a child who will bring back the golden age. Who Virgil meant is still debated; the poem is dedicated to his friend Pollio, consul in 40 BC. Later Christian readers, among them the emperor Constantine, read it as a prophecy of Christ, which is one reason Virgil was so honored in the Middle Ages.

blocks.text: The Georgics: a poem about work

blocks.name: gb-georgics
blocks.cap: The four books of the Georgics, and the ten Eclogues.

blocks.html: Each book of the Georgics takes one part of farming, but the poem is not a manual. It is about how people should live. In Book I Virgil says the god Jupiter made farming hard on purpose, so that people would grow inventive: “toil conquered everything,” in his words labor omnia vicit improbus, hard, unrelenting toil. Book II praises the quiet life of the farmer, far from war and politics.

“Happy he who hath availed to know the causes of things” is, in Latin, felix qui potuit rerum cognoscere causas. Many readers think Virgil had in mind Lucretius, whose poem on atoms (the rung before this one) promised freedom from fear through knowing how nature works. Virgil then adds that the farmer who honors the country gods is blessed too.

Book IV describes the hive as a model community: the bees share their homes, work in turns, store food for winter and defend their ruler. Virgil, like all ancient writers, called the ruler of the hive a king; naturalists of the 1600s showed that it is a female, the queen. The book closes with a myth: the beekeeper Aristaeus loses his bees and learns that he must make amends for the death of Eurydice. Inside this story Virgil tells how Orpheus, her husband, went down to the underworld to bring her back, and lost her again by looking back too soon.

Treating the Georgics as a farming textbook. Some of its advice is sound and some is ancient lore that is wrong (for example, the old belief, which Virgil repeats, that a swarm can be born from the body of a dead bullock; bees come from eggs laid by the queen). Roman farmers had real handbooks, by Cato and Varro. Virgil wrote a poem about work, seasons and how to live well.

items: Pastoral poetry: the Eclogues set the pattern for centuries of shepherd poems in many languages, among them Milton’s Lycidas.
The dignity of work: the Georgics made farming a subject for great poetry. Dryden, who translated all of Virgil, called it “the best poem of the best poet.”
Familiar words: “Love conquers all” (omnia vincit Amor) comes from the tenth Eclogue.

blocks.html:
🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

Rome had been at war with itself, off and on, since before Virgil was born. The Georgics praise Italy and pray for a ruler who will bring peace, and Book I ends with the bad omens around the murder of Julius Caesar in 44 BC and a world turned upside down: “so many wars, so many faces of crime.” An ancient life of Virgil says he read the finished poem aloud to Octavian in 29 BC, over four days, with Maecenas taking over when the poet’s voice grew tired.

items: Is hard work a curse, or a gift that makes us grow? Virgil seems to say both.
Is the quiet country life happier than the life of a city, or of fame? Or is that a dream of people who do not farm?
What can a community of animals, like bees, teach people? Where does the comparison break down?

blocks.html: Virgil’s Aeneid, the next rung, turned from fields to empire. Augustine, later in this era, read the fourth Eclogue in the light of Christian faith. Much later, English poets of the 1700s wrote whole “georgics” of their own, and writers on country life kept returning to Virgil’s question of how working the land shapes a person.

💬 Talk about it together

  1. Which weather signs have you noticed yourself? Do any of Virgil’s work where you live?
  2. Virgil says farmers are fortunate “did they know their own happiness.” Are there good things in your own life you might not notice?
  3. Is hard work something to escape, or something that makes us better? Can it be both?
  4. In the first Eclogue one neighbor keeps his farm and the other loses his. How should the lucky one treat the other?
  5. Bees share their work and their food. What jobs in your home are shared, and what would happen if no one did them?

blocks.html: A note for parents: The Aeneid is a war poem. There are battles and deaths, especially in Books 2, 10, 11 and 12, and Book 4 ends with Queen Dido taking her own life after Aeneas leaves her. The lesson summarizes these parts without detail. For young readers, Books 1, 3, 5 and 8 (the storm, the voyage, the games and the visit to the site of Rome) are the gentlest places to start.

🌱 For young readers

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.

Long ago the city of Troy was tricked by the Greeks and their wooden horse. One Trojan prince, Aeneas, escaped from the burning city. He carried his old father on his back and held his little son by the hand.

The gods told Aeneas to sail west and find a new home in Italy. The journey took seven years. He met storms, monsters and a queen who wanted him to stay. His people grew tired, and so did he. But he kept going, because he knew others were counting on him. The Romans told this story about themselves: Aeneas’s people became the Romans.

A Roman poet named Virgil wrote the story down as a long poem in twelve parts, called “books.” He called Aeneas pius, which means more than our word “pious.” It means faithful to your family, your country and your gods.

blocks.name: gb-voyage
blocks.cap: Follow Aeneas from Troy to Italy. Tap Next stop, or tap a number on the map.

blocks.html:
🧩 Try this

Make a shield of the future. In Book 8 the god Vulcan makes Aeneas a shield covered with pictures of Rome’s history, from its founding to the poet’s own day. Draw a round shield on paper and fill it with four or five scenes from your family’s story, from the oldest you know to today. Then tell someone the story, scene by scene.

There are battles in this story. If you read it with a grown-up, the voyage (Book 3), the boat race and games (Book 5) and the visit to the hills where Rome would one day stand (Book 8) are good places to begin.

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Publius Vergilius Maro, called Virgil in English, was born in 70 BC near Mantua in northern Italy and died in 19 BC. He grew up during Rome’s civil wars. When Octavian, Julius Caesar’s heir, defeated Antony and Cleopatra in 31 BC and became the emperor Augustus, Virgil had already written the Eclogues and the Georgics. He spent his last ten years on the Aeneid.

The poem gives Rome a founding story as grand as the Greeks’ Homer. Its first six books are a voyage, like the Odyssey; its last six are a war, like the Iliad. It also ties the hero to Augustus, whose family, the Julii, claimed descent from Aeneas’s son Iulus. Virgil died before he had finished revising it. An ancient life of Virgil says he asked for the poem to be burned, and that Augustus would not allow it. Dozens of lines are still unfinished, broken off halfway.
The Latin begins Arma virumque cano, “Arms and the man I sing.” In two words Virgil names his two models: arma, war, for the Iliad, and virum, the man, for the Odyssey.

head: Books
What happens
rows: Juno, who hates the Trojans, sends a storm. Aeneas lands near Carthage, a new city ruled by Queen Dido.
At Dido’s feast Aeneas tells of Troy’s fall and of his seven years of wandering.
Dido and Aeneas fall in love. Mercury, sent by Jupiter, reminds Aeneas of his duty. He leaves, and Dido dies in despair.
Funeral games in Sicily for his father, Anchises.
With the Sibyl of Cumae, Aeneas visits the underworld. Anchises shows him the great Romans of the future.
In Latium, King Latinus offers peace, but Juno stirs up war with the Rutulian prince Turnus. Aeneas finds allies at Pallanteum, where Rome will one day stand.
War in Italy. Evander’s son Pallas is killed by Turnus. In the last scene Aeneas defeats Turnus in single combat.

blocks.text: Pietas: the hero who carries others

blocks.html: Virgil’s word for Aeneas is pius. His pietas is loyalty to the gods, to his father and son, and to his people’s future. The poem’s most famous picture of it comes on the night Troy falls.
Duty costs him. He loses his wife Creusa in the flight from Troy. He leaves Dido, whom he loves. Leading tired people, he hides his own fear, as in his speech to the crew after the storm in Book 1.

Virgil’s Latin for the last idea is famous: forsan et haec olim meminisse iuvabit, “perhaps one day it will be a pleasure to remember even these things.” Readers have quoted it in hard times for two thousand years.
In the underworld, Anchises shows Aeneas a parade of future Romans and tells him what Rome’s gift to the world will be.

Readers disagree about how to take passages like this. Some read the Aeneid as a celebration of Rome and of Augustus. Others point to how much grief the poem gives to the losers: Dido, Turnus, and young men on both sides who die in the war. Many find both voices in it, and think Virgil meant them to be heard together.

Thinking Virgil invented Aeneas. Aeneas is already a Trojan hero in Homer’s Iliad, where a god predicts that he and his descendants will survive Troy. Roman writers had linked him with Rome’s founding long before Virgil. Virgil’s achievement was the poem, not the legend.

items: Schools: the Aeneid was the main Latin schoolbook for centuries, in Roman times and long after. Augustine, later on this ladder, learned it as a boy.
Dante: in the Divine Comedy, Virgil himself is Dante’s guide through Hell and up the mountain of Purgatory.
Words: phrases like “I fear the Greeks, even bearing gifts” (Laocoön’s warning about the wooden horse, Book 2) and “the tears of things” (lacrimae rerum, Book 1) came into many languages.

blocks.html:
🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

blocks.text: Context: an epic for a new age

blocks.html: Virgil wrote after a century of civil wars, when Augustus was building a new order while claiming to restore the old Republic. The poem reaches back to the past to explain the present: Book 6 names Augustus, and the shield in Book 8 shows his victory at Actium in 31 BC. Virgil also received the patronage of Augustus’s friend Maecenas. Whether this makes the poem propaganda, or a poet’s honest hopes and doubts about his age, is one of the oldest debates about it.

The poem ends abruptly. Turnus, beaten, asks for mercy, and Aeneas almost spares him. Then he sees the belt Turnus took from young Pallas, whom Aeneas had promised to protect, and in anger he kills him. The poem stops there, with no wedding, no founding and no peace. Some readers see justice, others a hero failing his father’s advice “to spare the conquered.” Virgil leaves the reader to decide.

items: When duty and love pull in opposite directions, how should a person choose? Was Aeneas right to leave Dido?
Can a story that celebrates a country also be honest about what its rise cost other people?
Is it fair to judge an ancient hero by our standards, or only by his own?

blocks.html: Augustine, in the Confessions, regrets that as a boy he wept for Dido and not for his own soul. In the City of God he quotes Virgil often, and argues against the hope that any earthly city, Rome included, will last forever. Dante made Virgil his guide. Milton’s Paradise Lost, much later on this ladder, opens as an epic in the same grand tradition, and the poet Tennyson called Virgil “lord of language.”

💬 Talk about it together

  1. Aeneas carries his father and leads his son. What do you owe to the people older and younger than you in your family?
  2. Was Aeneas right to leave Dido to go on with his mission? What would you have done?
  3. “Perhaps one day it will be a pleasure to remember even these things.” Is there a hard time you are glad, now, to remember?
  4. Virgil asked for the poem to be burned because it was unfinished. Why do you think Augustus saved it? Was he right?
  5. Which matters more in a leader: being brave, or being faithful to the people who depend on him?
  6. The poem makes the reader feel for Rome’s enemies too. Why might a poet do that in a poem about his own country?

blocks.html: A note for parents: Plutarch’s lives include wars, plots and violent deaths, told plainly but without much gore. This lesson summarizes those parts. The stories of Alexander and his horse, Solon and the rich king, Aristides “the Just” and Demosthenes practicing his speeches are good places for young readers to start.

Choose a path

  • 🌱 For young readers
  • 📖 For teens and adults
  • 🔭 Going deeper

🌱 For young readers

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.

Plutarch was a Greek who lived about 1,900 years ago, when Greece was part of the Roman Empire. He wrote short life stories of famous people. He put them in pairs, one Greek and one Roman, so readers could compare them: who was braver, who was wiser, who was fairer.
Plutarch cared most about character: what a person is like inside. He said that a small thing, like a joke or a quick answer, can show more about someone than a great battle.

Here is one of his stories. A wild horse named Bucephalus was brought to King Philip of Macedon. No one could ride it, and the king was about to send it away. His young son Alexander noticed that the horse was afraid of its own shadow. He turned the horse to face the sun, so the shadow fell behind it, calmed it with gentle strokes, and rode it. His father said Macedonia would be too small for him. Alexander grew up to be Alexander the Great.

🧩 Try this

Write a parallel life. Choose two people you admire, perhaps a grandparent and a hero from a book. Draw a line down a page. On each side, write one story that shows what that person is like. At the bottom, write how they are alike and how they differ. That is what Plutarch did.

blocks.name: gb-parallel-lives
blocks.cap: Choose a pair. The bars show when each person lived, and when Plutarch lived.

blocks.html:
📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Plutarch (c. AD 46–c. 120) lived all his life in the small town of Chaeronea in central Greece, though he studied at Athens, visited Rome and Egypt, and held the Roman citizenship. For many years he was a priest at Apollo’s temple at Delphi, not far from his home. He wrote a great many essays on ethics, religion and education, later collected as the Moralia, and his most famous work, the Parallel Lives.

The Lives pair a Greek with a Roman: Theseus with Romulus, Lycurgus with Numa, Pericles with Fabius Maximus, Alexander with Julius Caesar, Demosthenes with Cicero, and more. Twenty-two pairs survive, with four single lives; one pair is lost. After most pairs Plutarch adds a short comparison of the two. This rung looks at the Greek side; the next rung looks at the Romans.

blocks.name: gb-parallel-lives
blocks.cap: Plutarch’s pairs on a time line. Some lived centuries apart; Plutarch paired them for their character, not their dates.

blocks.html: At the start of the Life of Alexander, Plutarch explains what he is doing.

Plutarch’s method: a life is a moral portrait. He tells the deeds, but he chooses the details, the sayings, habits and small choices, that show what a person was like, so that readers can learn which qualities to copy and which to avoid.
In the Life of Pericles Plutarch says we admire a fine statue without wanting to become a sculptor, but good actions are different: they make us want to act the same way.

items: Lycurgus, Sparta’s lawgiver, whose rules trained citizens in hardship and discipline. Plutarch admits that almost nothing about him is certain.

Solon, who gave Athens fairer laws. Plutarch tells how the rich king Croesus asked Solon who was the happiest man, and Solon would call no one happy until his life had ended well. Plutarch says some doubt the meeting could have happened, but he keeps it because it fits Solon’s character.
Themistocles, who built the fleet that beat the Persians at Salamis in 480 BC, and was later exiled by his own city.

Aristides “the Just.” When Athens voted on exiling him, a farmer who could not write asked him, not knowing who he was, to write “Aristides” on the voting shard. Asked why, the farmer said he was tired of hearing him called “the Just.” Aristides wrote it.
Pericles, who led Athens in its golden age and had the Parthenon built.
Demosthenes, who as a young man trained his weak voice by speaking with pebbles in his mouth, and became Athens’s greatest orator.
Alexander the Great, from the horse Bucephalus to the conquest of Persia.

blocks.html: One more Alexander story shows Plutarch’s eye for a telling moment. The young king visits the philosopher Diogenes, who lived with almost nothing, and finds him lying in the sun.

Reading Plutarch as a modern historian. He wrote centuries after most of his subjects, used many sources of uneven quality, and sometimes repeats legends because they show character. Historians still use him, but they check him against other evidence. He himself tells readers when a story is doubtful.

items: Shakespeare took the plots of Julius Caesar, Antony and Cleopatra and Coriolanus from Sir Thomas North’s English Plutarch (1579), often following North’s wording closely.
Founders and leaders read him for examples: Montaigne loved him, and many of the American founders knew his heroes well.
Biography as we know it, a life told to show a person’s character, owes more to Plutarch than to anyone else.

blocks.html:
🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

blocks.text: Context: a Greek in a Roman world

blocks.html: By Plutarch’s day Greece had been ruled by Rome for two centuries. Pairing the two peoples was a quiet argument: Greece had heroes and lawgivers to set beside any Roman, and the two cultures belonged together. Plutarch had Roman friends of high rank, and he dedicated the Lives to one of them, Sosius Senecio.

items: Can we learn to be good by reading about good people? Or do we copy the exciting bad ones instead?
Is a small habit a truer sign of character than a great deed?
Solon would call no one happy until the end of his life. Was he right?
Is it fair to compare two people who lived centuries apart, in very different worlds?

blocks.html: Montaigne, later on this ladder, named Plutarch and Seneca as the two authors he read most. Shakespeare turned Plutarch’s Romans into drama. Boswell’s Life of Johnson, in the 18th-century era of this ladder, took Plutarch’s idea further: a life told through a person’s talk and small habits, day by day.

💬 Talk about it together

  1. Plutarch says a joke or a quick answer can show character better than a battle. What small thing someone did once showed you what they were really like?
  2. Alexander saw that the horse feared its shadow. What does that story tell you about him?
  3. Diogenes asked a king only to step out of his sunlight. Why did Alexander admire him for that?
  4. Why might the farmer have been tired of hearing Aristides called “the Just”? Is it easy to like someone who is always praised?
  5. Whose life would you want written down as an example? Whose as a warning?

blocks.html: A note for parents: The Roman lives tell of civil wars, political murders and battles, including the assassination of Julius Caesar and the deaths of Cicero, Antony and Cleopatra. The lesson names these events without detail. Young readers can start with Romulus and Remus, Caesar and the pirates, and Cato the Elder’s plain living.

Choose a path

  • 📖 For teens and adults

🌱 For young readers

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.

The Greek writer Plutarch paired each famous Greek with a famous Roman. His Romans include Romulus, who by legend founded Rome; Cato, a stern old farmer-statesman; Cicero, the great speaker; and Julius Caesar, the general who made himself master of Rome.

One of Plutarch’s stories: when Caesar was a young man, pirates captured his ship and asked for a ransom of twenty talents of silver. Caesar laughed and said he was worth at least fifty. While his friends gathered the money, he lived among the pirates for thirty-eight days, joined their games, made them listen to his poems, and told them to be quiet when he wanted to sleep. Plutarch tells it to show how bold and sure of himself Caesar was, even then.

🧩 Try this

Small things show character. Plutarch thought little moments tell us who a person is. Think of someone you know well. Write down one small thing they once did or said that shows what they are like: kind, brave, funny, patient. Read it to your family and see if they can guess who it is.

blocks.name: gb-parallel-lives
blocks.cap: Choose a pair: the Greek on top, the Roman below, Plutarch at the bottom.

blocks.html:
📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Plutarch (c. AD 46–c. 120) wrote his Parallel Lives when Rome ruled the whole Mediterranean. His Romans run from the legendary founders, Romulus and Numa, through the heroes of the early Republic, such as Camillus and Coriolanus, to the men of the last century of the Republic: Marius and Sulla, Pompey and Crassus, Cato the Younger, Cicero, Caesar, Brutus and Antony. Read together, these lives tell how the Republic grew great and then tore itself apart in civil wars.

blocks.name: gb-parallel-lives
blocks.cap: Each Roman beside his Greek partner, and Plutarch’s own lifetime for scale.

blocks.html: Plutarch tells Caesar’s life through vivid moments. Crossing the Alps on his way to govern a province, Caesar passed a poor mountain village, and his companions joked about whether even there men fought to be first.
Years later, after a lightning campaign in Asia Minor in 47 BC, he reported his victory to a friend in Rome.
The three Latin words are veni, vidi, vici. Plutarch, writing in Greek, admires how they sound alike and how short they are: the style matches the speed of the campaign.
And on his last day, in 44 BC:

That day a group of senators led by Brutus and Cassius killed Caesar in the senate meeting. Plutarch tells it in several lives (Caesar, Brutus, Cicero, Antony) from different sides, so readers see one event through several characters.

items: Romulus, raised with his twin Remus, by legend, by a she-wolf; he founds Rome (by tradition in 753 BC). Plutarch reports several versions and admits much is fable.
Coriolanus, a proud general who, driven out of Rome, leads an enemy army against it, and turns back only when his mother Volumnia pleads with him.
Cato the Elder, who wore plain clothes, worked in the fields beside his slaves and fought luxury as censor.
Tiberius and Gaius Gracchus, brothers who tried to give land to poor citizens and were killed in political violence; Plutarch pairs them with two reforming kings of Sparta.
Cicero, the orator, who spoke for the Republic and was killed in the proscriptions after Caesar’s death.
Antony, Caesar’s friend, whose alliance with Cleopatra ended in defeat at Actium in 31 BC. Plutarch offers his life, with that of Demetrius, as a warning.

blocks.html: Thinking Plutarch takes sides like a party writer. He admires Cato the Younger and Brutus for their principles, but he also praises Caesar’s mercy to his enemies and blames the violence on all sides. His judgments are moral (was this man brave, honest, self-controlled?) rather than political.

items: Shakespeare built Julius Caesar, Antony and Cleopatra and Coriolanus on North’s Plutarch. The soothsayer’s warning comes straight from the Life of Caesar.
Words and phrases like “the die is cast” (Caesar at the Rubicon) and “veni, vidi, vici” reached us largely through Plutarch and the Roman biographer Suetonius.
Republics: later readers studied these lives to learn how a free government can fall into one-man rule.

blocks.html:
🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

blocks.text: Context: looking back on the Republic

blocks.html: Plutarch wrote under emperors such as Trajan, more than a century after the Republic fell. He could look back calmly on its last generation and ask what in each man’s character led to the civil wars. He used many sources, some now lost, including Cicero’s own writings and Caesar’s accounts of his wars.

items: Is ambition, like Caesar’s wish to be first, a virtue or a danger? When does it become one or the other?
Coriolanus turned back for his mother’s sake. What makes a person listen when nothing else works?
Can a good person do a wrong thing for a good reason? How does Plutarch judge Brutus?
Why might it help to read about one event, like Caesar’s death, from several people’s points of view?

blocks.html: Tacitus, the next rung, tells what happened after the Republic: the rule of the first emperors, seen through a senator’s eyes. Shakespeare turned Plutarch’s Romans into plays. Machiavelli, Montesquieu and Rousseau, later on this ladder, all drew lessons about republics from these same Roman lives.

💬 Talk about it together

  1. Caesar told the pirates he was worth more ransom. Was that brave, proud, or both?
  2. “I had rather be the first man among these fellows than the second man in Rome.” Would you rather be first in a small place or second in a big one? Why?
  3. Coriolanus’s mother changed his mind when no one else could. Who can change your mind?
  4. Cato lived plainly though he was important. Does having more make it harder to live well?
  5. Plutarch tells Caesar’s death from several sides. Why might that be fairer than one account?

The lesson names these events without detail. Young readers can start with the shape of the story and with the question Tacitus raises: how do you write history fairly?

Choose a path

  • 🌱 For young readers
  • 📖 For teens and adults
  • 🔭 Going deeper

🌱 For young readers

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.

Tacitus was a Roman senator who wrote the history of the first emperors after Augustus. He lived through hard times himself: under one emperor, senators were afraid to speak their minds. When better times came, he wrote down what had happened, so that people would remember.

Tacitus promised to write about the past “without anger and without partiality”, which means without letting his own feelings, or his friends and enemies, bend the truth. That is a hard promise to keep, and readers still argue about whether he kept it.

🧩 Try this

Two sides of one story. Think of a small argument that happened in your family or class, such as who got the last cookie. Write what happened in two short versions: one by someone who was upset, one by someone calm and fair. Underline the words in each version that show feelings (“grabbed,” “selfish,” “just took one”). Which version would a good historian trust more, and why?

blocks.name: gb-emperors
blocks.cap: The emperors Tacitus wrote about. Tap a bar to learn about each one. Some parts of his books are lost.

blocks.html:
📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Cornelius Tacitus (c. AD 56–c. 120) came from a family outside Rome, probably in Gaul or northern Italy, and rose through the offices of state to become consul in AD 97 and later governor of the province of Asia. He married the daughter of Agricola, the general who governed Britain. He served under the emperor Domitian (AD 81–96), whose last years were a time of fear for the senate, and began writing when Nerva and Trajan came to power.

He wrote two great histories. The Histories (written around AD 100–110) told the story from the civil war of AD 69 to Domitian’s death in 96. The Annals, written later, went back to AD 14 and covered the emperors Tiberius, Caligula, Claudius and Nero. Neither survives complete: we have about a third of the Histories and a little over half of the Annals.

blocks.name: gb-emperors
blocks.cap: The emperors from AD 14 to 96, and how much of Tacitus survives for each. Tap a bar.

blocks.html: The Annals open with a short sketch of Rome from the kings to Augustus, then Tacitus explains why a new history is needed.

In Latin the promise is four words: sine ira et studio, “without anger and without partiality” (or zeal). Tacitus names the two ways history goes wrong: flattery while a ruler lives, and hatred after he dies.
The Histories begin the same way, then warn the reader what is coming.

blocks.text: What the Annals and Histories tell

items: Tiberius (AD 14–37): Germanicus, the popular general, dies in the East; the ambitious minister Sejanus rises and falls; treason trials make the senate afraid. Tacitus shows an able ruler growing more suspicious and remote.
Claudius (41–54): the surviving books show a court run by his wives and freed slaves, and the conquest of Britain.

Nero (54–68): good early years under the advice of Seneca; then crimes within his own family, the great fire of Rome in AD 64 and a failed plot against him. Tacitus records that Nero blamed the fire on the Christians, one of the earliest mentions of Christ by a writer who was not a Christian.
The year of the four emperors (AD 69): Galba, Otho and Vitellius each seize power and fall within months, until Vespasian ends the civil war.
Rome’s frontiers: the revolt of the British queen Boudica (AD 60–61), wars in Germany and Armenia, and a revolt on the Rhine.

blocks.html: Tacitus is famous for short, sharp sentences that pack a judgment into a few words. Of Galba he wrote that everyone would have thought him fit to rule, had he never ruled. In the Annals he remarks that the more corrupt the state, the more numerous its laws (corruptissima re publica plurimae leges). He often reports what people suspected or rumored, which lets him hint at a judgment without stating it.

Taking every judgment in Tacitus as plain fact. He was a senator writing about emperors, and his sympathies lie with the senate. He sometimes reports a rumor and then lets it color the reader’s view. Historians compare him with other sources, such as the biographer Suetonius, inscriptions and coins. Most still regard him as the greatest Roman historian, and also as one who must be read carefully.

items: History writing: “without anger and without partiality” became a motto for historians, even those who think no one fully achieves it.
Freedom: readers in later centuries, living under kings, found in Tacitus a study of how power works, and how flattery and fear destroy free speech.
Survival: Books 1–6 of the Annals survive in a single medieval manuscript, and Books 11–16 with the Histories in another. Without them we would know far less about the first century AD.

blocks.html:
🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

blocks.text: Context: writing after a time of fear

blocks.html: In his short Agricola (AD 98), Tacitus says that under Domitian Romans lost the very memory of free speech, and that they would have lost memory itself if forgetting were as easy as keeping silent. His histories are, in part, an effort to remember. In the same book he gives a British chief a famous line about Roman conquest: “they make a desert and call it peace” (solitudinem faciunt, pacem appellant). Ancient historians often wrote such speeches themselves, and Tacitus’s willingness to voice Rome’s enemies is part of what makes him interesting.

items: Can anyone write about people they lived through, or suffered under, without anger or partiality?
Is it fair for a historian to report rumors? When is a rumor itself an important fact?
Why might people under a powerful ruler stop telling the truth, even when no one forces them to lie?
Tacitus served Domitian and did well under him, and later wrote against him. What should a good person do under a bad government?

blocks.html: Gibbon’s Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire, later on this ladder, admired Tacitus and took up the story where the great Roman historians left off. Montesquieu drew on him for his studies of Roman greatness and of liberty. Readers have long disagreed over whether Tacitus teaches how to resist tyranny or how to survive it.

💬 Talk about it together

  1. What does it mean to write “without anger and without partiality”? Is it possible?
  2. Why might history written while a ruler is alive be different from history written after he dies?
  3. When you hear two versions of the same story, how do you decide which to trust?
  4. Tacitus says fear made people stop speaking freely. Have you ever kept quiet because you were afraid of what others would think? What happened?
  5. Much of Tacitus is lost. What would you most want to be remembered from our own time, and how could we make sure it survives?

🌱 For young readers

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.

Epictetus (say it ep-ick-TEE-tus) was born a slave, about 1,950 years ago. He walked with a limp. But he grew up to be one of the most famous teachers in the Roman world, and an emperor read his lessons.

His big idea was simple. Some things are up to us, and some things are not. What we think, what we choose and how we act are up to us. The weather, other people’s opinions and whether we win are not. Epictetus said that if we put our worry and effort into the things that are up to us, and accept the rest calmly, we can be free and steady inside, even when things go wrong.

blocks.name: gb-up-to-us
blocks.cap: Sort each card. Is it up to you or not? Then press Check.

blocks.html:
🧩 Try this

The two-column worry list. Fold a paper in half. On the left write “Up to me,” on the right “Not up to me.” Write down three things that are bothering you this week, each in the right column. For each one on the left, write one small thing you can do. For each one on the right, write a sentence about how you could face it calmly. Talk it over with a grown-up.
Epictetus used the word Zeus, or God, often, and taught that the world is guided by a wise providence. That was part of his Stoic faith.

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Epictetus was born around AD 50 at Hierapolis in Phrygia (in today’s Turkey) and was a slave in Rome in the household of Epaphroditus, a powerful freedman of the emperor Nero. He was lame; one story blamed a cruel master, but an ancient commentator says he was weak and lame from early on. His master let him study with the Stoic teacher Musonius Rufus. Freed, he taught philosophy in Rome until the emperor Domitian banished the philosophers from the city, around AD 93. He then opened a school at Nicopolis in western Greece, where students came from all over the empire, and he died there around AD 135.

Like Socrates, he wrote nothing. A student, Arrian of Nicomedia (later a governor and historian), took down his talks. Four books of these Discourses survive out of eight, and Arrian also made a short summary, the Encheiridion or Handbook, which means something you keep “in hand.”

blocks.text: Up to us, and not up to us

blocks.html: The Handbook opens with Epictetus’s central idea.

The Greek phrase is eph’ hēmin, “up to us.” What is up to us is our prohairesis, our power of choice: how we judge things, what we want and avoid, what we decide to do. Everything else, even our own bodies, depends at least partly on things outside us.

blocks.name: gb-up-to-us
blocks.cap: Eight cards. Sort them by Epictetus’s rule, then check.

blocks.text: It is our opinions that disturb us

blocks.html: Epictetus does not say that bad things are not bad, or that people should not try to change the world. He says that our distress comes from the judgment we add to events, and that the judgment is ours to examine. A student who fails a test feels the failure; what turns it into “I am worthless” is an opinion, and opinions can be tested.
In the first of the Discourses, Epictetus imagines a man threatened by a tyrant, and shows what such a man should keep ready in his mind.
Epictetus’s teaching can be set out as a simple argument. The premises are his; whether they are true is the real question.

head: Statement
rows: Premise 1
Only what is up to us can be truly good or bad for us.
Premise 2
Other people’s opinions of us are not up to us.
Conclusion
So other people’s opinions of us are not truly good or bad for us.
blocks.cap: The form is valid: if both premises are true, the conclusion must be. Critics question Premise 1.

blocks.html: Thinking Stoics try to feel nothing. Epictetus wants his students to love their families, keep their duties and act justly. What he tries to remove are the disturbing passions that come from false judgments, such as treating money or praise as if they were the most important things in life. His goal is calm, steady action, not coldness.

items: Marcus Aurelius, the next rung, thanks his teacher Rusticus for lending him the notes of Epictetus’s lectures.
Later readers, Christian and not, used the Handbook as a guide to self-discipline for centuries; it was adapted for monks in the Middle Ages.
Modern psychology: the founders of cognitive therapy, Albert Ellis and Aaron Beck, named Epictetus’s saying about opinions as one source of their idea that how we interpret events shapes how we feel.

blocks.html:
🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

Stoicism began in Athens around 300 BC with Zeno of Citium, who taught in a painted porch, the stoa, which gave the school its name. By Epictetus’s day it was the leading philosophy among educated Romans; Seneca, Nero’s adviser, was a Stoic too. Epictetus taught it as a way of life rather than as a set of theories: daily practice, self-examination and training in how to respond to events. He also taught that all people share in reason and are akin to God, so that a slave and an emperor are equally capable of freedom.

items: Is anything outside our control truly good or bad for us? What about health, friends or justice?
If we accept what we cannot change, will we stop trying to change things that are wrong?
Can a person in chains be free? What kind of freedom would that be?
Is Epictetus’s idea comforting, demanding, or both?

blocks.html: Marcus Aurelius turned these lessons into an emperor’s private notebook. Augustine, later in this era, honored the Stoics’ seriousness but held that true peace comes from God’s grace, not from the will alone. Pascal, in the 17th century, praised Epictetus for seeing human greatness and blamed him for not seeing human weakness. Montaigne drew on the Stoics in his essays on how to face pain and death.

💬 Talk about it together

  1. Name something that went wrong this week. What part of it was up to you, and what part was not?
  2. Epictetus says it is our opinion about a thing that disturbs us. Can you think of a time when changing how you thought about something changed how you felt?
  3. Is what other people think of you up to you? Should you care about it at all?
  4. Epictetus was a slave who taught that he was free inside. What do you think he meant?
  5. If you accept the things you cannot change, how do you decide which things those are?

🌱 For young readers

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.

Marcus Aurelius was emperor of Rome about 1,850 years ago. He was the most powerful man in the world. But he did not want to be proud or cruel. Every day he wrote notes to himself in a little notebook: reminders to be fair, patient, kind and calm.

He never meant anyone else to read it. Today we call it the Meditations. In it he tells himself things like: Each morning, expect to meet some grumpy or unkind people. Remember that they are your brothers and sisters, and that we are made to help each other, like two hands.
One of his favorite exercises was to imagine looking down from very high up, so that his worries looked small. Try it below.

blocks.name: gb-view-from-above
blocks.cap: Slide to zoom out, from you to the whole of time. Each step has one of Marcus’s thoughts.

blocks.html:
🧩 Try this

A thank-you list, Marcus style. The first part of the Meditations is a list of people Marcus was grateful to, and what he learned from each: from his grandfather, good manners and a calm temper; from his mother, kindness and simple living. Write your own list: five people, and one good thing you learned from each. You might give one of them a copy.

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Marcus Aurelius (AD 121–180) was adopted, at the emperor Hadrian’s wish, by Hadrian’s successor Antoninus Pius, and became emperor himself in AD 161. As a young man he studied rhetoric with Fronto and philosophy with the Stoic Junius Rusticus. His reign was hard: a plague spread through the empire, and he spent most of his last ten years on campaign against German tribes along the Danube. He died in AD 180, and his son Commodus succeeded him.

The Meditations are twelve short books of notes, written in Greek, mostly in the 170s. The oldest manuscripts call them ta eis heauton, “to himself.” Two of the books carry notes on where they were written: one “among the Quadi at the Granua,” a river on the frontier, and one at Carnuntum, an army base on the Danube. They are not a treatise. They are an emperor reminding himself, again and again, how he wants to live.

blocks.text: Book I: what I learned from others

blocks.html: Book I is a list of debts: what Marcus learned from his family, teachers and friends. From Rusticus, for instance:

Three Stoic ideas in one paragraph: people do wrong from ignorance of what is good; no one can harm my character but me; and all people are kin, made to work together. Marcus does not pretend difficult people are pleasant. He prepares himself to meet them without anger.

Marcus often imagines his life from a great height or across great stretches of time: the whole earth a point, Europe and Asia corners of the universe, the busy people of earlier reigns all gone. The exercise is not meant to make life seem worthless. It shrinks fame, anger and worry down to size, so that what is left (acting justly, now) stands out.

blocks.name: gb-view-from-above
blocks.cap: Zoom out step by step. Each level gives one of Marcus’s thoughts, in our words, with book and section.

blocks.html: Reading the Meditations as advice to give up and withdraw. Marcus worked very hard: he judged cases, ran the empire and led armies in his last years. His notes keep turning back to duty: do the work in front of you, as well as you can, for the common good, and do not wait for praise.

items: A rare record: we have almost no other private writing by a Roman emperor. Here a ruler examines his own faults.

The philosopher-king: Plato had hoped that philosophers might rule. Later writers often pointed to Marcus as the nearest example, while noting that he still fought wars, and that he left the throne to a son who ruled badly.
Lasting readers: the Meditations have stayed in print in many languages, and are read today by people from soldiers to students who want a daily practice of self-command.

blocks.html:
🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

blocks.text: Context: a Stoic on the throne

blocks.html: Marcus learned Stoicism largely from Epictetus’s teaching, which he read in Arrian’s notes. Like Epictetus, he believed that a wise reason (which he calls nature, God or the gods) orders the world, that everything changes, and that virtue is the only true good. He writes about these beliefs as his own convictions and also, at times, wonders whether the world is ordered by providence or is only atoms, and concludes that either way he must act justly. His reign also saw the persecution of Christians in some places; how much he himself was responsible is debated by historians.

items: Can a powerful person stay humble? What helped Marcus try?
Is it good to remind yourself often that you will die? Why did Marcus think so?
Marcus says no one can harm your character but you. Is that true, or are we shaped by how others treat us?
Why write notes to yourself? What would you put in your own notebook?

blocks.html: Plotinus, the next rung, began teaching in Rome about sixty years after Marcus died, and turned inward in a different way: toward a union of the soul with the One. Augustine’s Confessions is also a book of self-examination, but written as a prayer to God. Montaigne’s essays, later on this ladder, made writing about oneself into a new kind of book.

💬 Talk about it together

  1. Marcus expected to meet difficult people each day. How might expecting it help you stay calm?
  2. Who taught you something important? What did they teach you?
  3. Where is your “inner retreat,” the quiet place in your mind you can go to?
  4. When you imagine a problem from very far away, does it look smaller? Does that help, or not?
  5. Marcus was the most powerful man in the world and still wrote reminders to be humble. Why might powerful people need such reminders most?

🌱 For young readers

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.
Plotinus was a teacher who lived in Rome about 1,750 years ago. He loved the ideas of Plato, the great Greek thinker who lived six hundred years before him.

Plotinus pictured all of reality as being like light from the sun. At the center is a perfect source he called the One, or the Good. From it flows everything else, the way light flows from a lamp: first a great Mind, then Soul, then the living world we see. The farther from the source, the dimmer the light. And our souls, he taught, can turn around and travel back toward the light.

blocks.name: gb-emanation
blocks.cap: Tap a ring to read about it. Switch between “going out” and “coming back.”

blocks.html:
🧩 Try this

The fading light. In a dark room, shine a flashlight at a wall from close up, then step back a few steps at a time. Watch the spot grow bigger and dimmer. Plotinus used light like this as a picture of how everything comes from one source. Talk about it: what is the “source” of good things in your life?
Plotinus was shy about his body and his fame. He would not even let anyone paint his portrait. His friends had an artist come to his lectures and draw him from memory!

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Plotinus (c. AD 204–270) was probably born in Egypt, though he never told even his students where he came from. He studied philosophy in Alexandria for eleven years with a teacher named Ammonius Saccas. Hoping to learn the wisdom of Persia and India, he joined the emperor Gordian III’s army on a campaign to the East, which failed. In AD 244 he settled in Rome and taught there for the rest of his life. The emperor Gallienus admired him, and Plotinus once asked him to rebuild a ruined town in Campania as a “city of philosophers,” Platonopolis, to be run by Plato’s laws. Rivals at court stopped the plan.

His student Porphyry collected his 54 treatises after his death, arranged them in six groups of nine, and published them around AD 300 with a Life of Plotinus. The groups are the Enneads, from the Greek ennea, “nine.” Porphyry put the ethical treatises first, then the world, then the soul, Intellect, and finally the One.

Plotinus taught that reality has levels. At the top is the One, which is perfectly simple and beyond anything we can say of it. From the One comes Intellect (nous), a divine Mind that thinks all the Forms, Plato’s eternal patterns. From Intellect comes Soul, which gives life and order to the world of bodies. At the farthest edge is matter, which has no form of its own. Each level flows from the one above without the higher one losing anything, as a fire gives off heat or the sun gives light.

blocks.name: gb-emanation
blocks.cap: Plotinus’s levels of reality, drawn as light from a source. Tap a ring; switch the direction.

blocks.html: Two movements: procession, the outflow from the One down to matter, and return, the soul’s turning back. The return is the purpose of philosophy for Plotinus: through virtue, the love of beauty and contemplation, the soul rises to Intellect and, at rare moments, to union with the One.
The treatise On Beauty (Ennead I.6) was the first Plotinus wrote, and the most read. It begins with ordinary beauty and climbs.

Plotinus then argues against a common view of his day, that beauty is just symmetry, the right proportion of parts. If that were so, he says, a single color or a flash of lightning could not be beautiful, since they have no parts. Beauty, for him, is the presence of form: a thing is beautiful when it shares in an order that comes from above. Near the end he tells the reader how to see the highest beauty.

If everything flows from the Good, where does evil come from? Plotinus answers that evil is not a power of its own. It is a lack, like darkness, which is only the absence of light. Matter, at the far edge where form gives out, is the limit of this lack, and the soul goes wrong when it turns its attention away from what is above toward what is below.

Calling Plotinus a “Neoplatonist” as if he thought he was starting something new. The word was invented by modern scholars. Plotinus saw himself as explaining Plato, and he often says his views are only Plato’s, rightly understood.

items: Augustine, two rungs on, read “books of the Platonists” in Latin in Milan, very likely including Plotinus. In the Confessions he says they helped him think of God as spiritual and of evil as a lack of good.
Medieval thought: through Augustine and later writers, Plotinus’s picture of a ladder of being and of light flowing from God shaped Christian, Jewish and Islamic philosophy.
The Renaissance: Marsilio Ficino translated the Enneads into Latin (published 1492), and artists and poets took up Plotinus’s idea of beauty as a trace of a higher world.

blocks.html:
🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

blocks.text: Context: philosophy as a way to God

blocks.html: In the third century the Roman Empire was in crisis: many emperors were killed, the frontiers were attacked and plagues returned. Educated people turned to philosophy and religion for a path to the divine. Plotinus offered one through reason and inner discipline rather than ritual. Porphyry writes that Plotinus reached union with the One four times in the six years Porphyry was with him. These are Plotinus’s beliefs and Porphyry’s report of them; the lesson presents them as such.

items: Is beauty only in the eye of the beholder, or is it something real that we discover?
Can something give without losing anything? What examples can you think of (light, a teacher’s knowledge, a song)?
Is evil a thing in itself, or only the absence of good?
What does it mean to “chisel your own statue”? Is becoming good more like sculpting or like growing?

blocks.html: Augustine took up Plotinus’s answer about evil and his inward turn, but placed them within Christian faith in a personal God and in grace. Thomas Aquinas, in the Middle Ages, knew Neoplatonic ideas through Augustine and other writers. Much later, poets of the Romantic era found in Plotinus a philosopher of beauty and of the mind’s ascent.

💬 Talk about it together

  1. What is the most beautiful thing you have seen or heard this week? Was it beautiful because of its parts, or something more?
  2. Plotinus would not have his portrait painted. Why might someone not want a picture of himself? Do you agree with him?
  3. What would you “chisel away” from your own statue, if you could?
  4. Plotinus says the eye must become sunlike to see the sun. What do you think he means for people?
  5. Light gets dimmer the farther it travels. Where in life do good things get weaker as they pass from person to person, and where do they get stronger?

🌱 For young readers

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.

Nicomachus lived about 1,900 years ago in Gerasa, a Roman city in what is now Jordan. He wrote a short book about the personalities of numbers: which are even and which odd, which can be split into equal rows, and which are special in other ways.
Some numbers make pictures. Put dots in rows of 1, 2, 3, 4 and you get a triangle of 10 dots. Make rows of 3, 3 and 3 and you get a square of 9. Nicomachus called these triangular and square numbers.

blocks.name: gb-figurate
blocks.cap: Pick a kind and slide n to grow the picture.

blocks.html:
🧩 Try this

Dots and beans. With dried beans or pennies, build the triangles for 1, 3, 6, 10 and 15. Put two triangles side by side: what shape do you get? Now build squares 1, 4, 9 and 16. How many beans do you add each time to go from one square to the next? (Try the odd numbers.)

Nicomachus also liked perfect numbers. The numbers that divide 6 evenly, apart from 6, are 1, 2 and 3. Add them: 1 + 2 + 3 = 6. The number is exactly the sum of its parts! The next perfect number is 28. They are rare: there are only four below 10,000.

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Nicomachus (c. AD 60–c. 120) came from Gerasa, a prosperous city of the Roman province of Syria (today Jerash in Jordan). He was a Pythagorean: a follower of the old tradition, going back to Pythagoras in the 500s BC, that saw number as the key to music, the heavens and the order of the world. He also wrote a short handbook on music theory.

His problem was teaching. Euclid had proved results about numbers, but his Elements are hard going. Nicomachus wrote an introduction for students: definitions, names and many worked examples, with no proofs. It became one of the most copied textbooks in history. Boethius adapted it into Latin around AD 500, and his version was the standard arithmetic of European schools for about a thousand years, as the first of the four mathematical arts (arithmetic, music, geometry and astronomy). Thabit ibn Qurra translated it into Arabic in the 800s.

head: Name
Meaning
Examples
rows: even-times even
keeps halving evenly all the way down to 1
even-times odd
halves once to an odd number
odd-times even
halves more than once, but not down to 1
prime and incomposite
an odd number measured only by the unit
secondary and composite
an odd number with another odd factor
blocks.cap: Nicomachus's names for kinds of numbers (Book I). He treats 2 as even-times even and lists primes among the odd numbers.

blocks.html: To find the odd primes he describes the method Eratosthenes, the librarian of Alexandria, had called the sieve. Nicomachus's book is our earliest surviving description of it.

blocks.title: Sifting to 50
blocks.q: Use the sieve to find the odd primes below 50.
steps: Write the odd numbers 3, 5, 7, …, 49.
Cross out every third one after 3 (9, 15, 21, 27, 33, 39, 45): the multiples of 3.
Cross out the multiples of 5 after 5 (25, 35); 15 and 45 are already gone.
Cross out the multiples of 7 after 7 (49; 21 and 35 are gone). Since $7 \times 7 = 49$ is the last square below 50, we can stop.

blocks.text: Too much, too little and just right

blocks.html: Nicomachus sorts numbers by adding up their parts (the smaller numbers that divide them exactly). If the parts add to less than the number, it is deficient; if more, superabundant; if exactly equal, perfect.

blocks.name: gb-perfect
blocks.cap: Each number is colored by whether its parts fall short, overshoot or land exactly. Press one to see its parts.

blocks.html: He gives the first four perfect numbers, 6, 28, 496 and 8,128, and a recipe for making more that is Euclid's IX.36 in other words: add 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 + … and, whenever the sum is prime, multiply it by the last number added.

Trusting every pattern Nicomachus states. He says there is one perfect number among the units, one among the tens, one among the hundreds and one among the thousands, and that they end alternately in 6 and 8. Both patterns fail. The fifth perfect number, 33,550,336, has eight digits, so there is none with five, six or seven; and the fifth and sixth (8,589,869,056) both end in 6. He saw the pattern in four examples and did not prove it. That is the difference between his book and Euclid's.

blocks.name: gb-figurate
blocks.cap: Triangular, square, pentagonal and oblong numbers, and the cubes built from odd numbers.

blocks.html: Book II arranges numbers as shapes made of points: polygonal numbers (triangular, square, pentagonal, …), oblong numbers (a side times one more: 2, 6, 12, 20), and solid numbers like pyramids and cubes. Along the way come neat facts: every square is the sum of two neighboring triangular numbers, and if you add the odd numbers in groups (1; 3 + 5; 7 + 9 + 11; …) you get the cubes 1, 8, 27, …

blocks.title: The cube of 4 from odd numbers
blocks.q: Which odd numbers add up to $4^3$ in Nicomachus's pattern?
steps: Groups so far: 1 | 3, 5 | 7, 9, 11. The fourth group takes the next four odd numbers.
They are 13, 15, 17 and 19.

blocks.title: Three kinds of mean
blocks.q: Find the arithmetic, geometric and harmonic means of 4 and 9 (where they are whole numbers).
steps: Arithmetic mean: halfway, $\frac{4 + 9}{2} = 6.5$.
Geometric mean: the number $g$ with $4 : g = g : 9$, so $g^2 = 36$, $g = 6$.
Harmonic mean: $\frac{2 \times 4 \times 9}{4 + 9} = \frac{72}{13} \approx 5.54$. Only the geometric mean is a whole number here.

blocks.html: The book ends with ten kinds of proportion. Nicomachus calls 6, 8, 9, 12 the "most perfect proportion": 9 is the arithmetic mean of 6 and 12, 8 is their harmonic mean, and the ratios 6 : 8 and 9 : 12 (3 : 4), 6 : 9 and 8 : 12 (2 : 3), and 6 : 12 (1 : 2) are the musical intervals of the fourth, the fifth and the octave.

blocks.text: What later mathematics kept, and what it changed

items: Kept: the sieve, figurate numbers, perfect and abundant numbers, and the means. Mathematicians still use the words abundant and deficient.
Dropped: the moral and religious meanings Nicomachus gave to numbers, such as calling equality the source of goodness. Those belong to his Pythagorean philosophy, not to arithmetic.

Changed: arithmetic since Fermat and Euler rests on proofs, not examples. The questions Nicomachus raised are still open in places: no one knows whether there are infinitely many perfect numbers, or any odd ones.

blocks.html:
🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

Nicomachus and Euclid cover some of the same ground, the kinds of numbers and the recipe for perfect numbers, but they work in different ways. Euclid proves each claim from definitions. Nicomachus shows examples, names the patterns and leaves it there. For teaching beginners his way has strengths: students see and count before they prove. But it lets mistakes in, as with his patterns for perfect numbers.

This is a lasting question in teaching mathematics: how much should beginners see and count, and how soon should they meet proofs? The medieval schools learned from Boethius's Nicomachus for centuries before Euclid's proofs came back into wide use.

For Nicomachus, number was the pattern in the mind of the maker of the world, and arithmetic was the first of the sciences because the others depend on it. Readers today can take or leave that philosophy, but the practical point survived: music is ratios of string lengths, astronomy is cycles and periods, and geometry needs measurement. Kepler, Galileo and Newton, later on this ladder, kept the conviction that nature is written in numbers, while dropping the number mysticism.

items: Is a pattern that holds for four examples likely to hold forever? How many examples would convince you?
Why do people give personalities and meanings to numbers (lucky numbers, unlucky numbers)?
Nicomachus's book was read for 1,000 years. What makes a textbook last?

blocks.html:
💬 Talk about it together

  1. Build the first five triangular numbers with beans. What do you add each time?
  2. Do you have a favorite number? What is special about it: is it even, odd, prime, square, triangular?
  3. Nicomachus guessed a pattern from four perfect numbers and was wrong. When have you guessed a pattern that turned out to break?
  4. Why might a teacher show examples first and proofs later? Is that how you like to learn?
  5. Nicomachus thought numbers explained music. Can you find the 1 : 2 ratio by plucking a string, then pressing it down at its middle?

🌱 For young readers

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.

Ptolemy was an astronomer who lived in Alexandria, in Egypt, about 1,900 years ago. He wrote a giant book that explained how to predict where the Sun, the Moon and the planets would be in the sky, years ahead. People used it for about 1,400 years.

Ptolemy thought the Earth stood still in the middle, with everything else going around it. The tricky part was the planets. Mars, for example, usually drifts slowly eastward against the stars, night after night. But every two years or so it slows down, goes backward for a few weeks, then turns forward again!

Ptolemy explained this with a circle on a circle. Mars rides around a small circle, and the center of the small circle rides around a big circle. When Mars is on the inside of its small circle, it seems to go backward.

blocks.name: gb-epicycle
blocks.cap: Watch Mars loop backward. Then switch to the Sun in the middle and see the same thing another way.

blocks.html:
🧩 Try this

Act it out. You need two people and a lamp for the Sun. One person (Earth) walks a small circle around the lamp; the other (Mars) walks a bigger circle, more slowly. Earth keeps pointing at Mars. When Earth overtakes Mars on the inside, Earth's arm swings backward for a while, though both are still walking forward. That is the backward loop!

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Claudius Ptolemy (c. AD 100–c. 170) worked in Alexandria under Roman rule. His observations date from AD 127 to 141. He called his great work the Mathematical Composition; Arabic translators called it al-majisti, "the greatest", which became Almagest in Latin. He also wrote major books on geography, optics, music theory and astrology.

The problem he faced was prediction. Greek astronomers had believed for centuries that heavenly motions must be built from uniform circles. Hipparchus (c. 190–c. 120 BC) had made this work for the Sun and Moon, but his books are lost. Nobody had produced a full, working theory for the planets, with tables anyone could use to compute their positions. Ptolemy did.

No public-domain English translation of the Almagest exists, so this lesson describes it in our own words, with no quotations. The standard English translation is G. J. Toomer's (1984); the Great Books set uses R. Catesby Taliaferro's (1952). Both are under copyright. Look for them in a library.

head: Books
Subject
rows: I–II
The heavens are a sphere and turn as one; the Earth is a sphere at the center, motionless, and tiny compared with the distance to the stars. A table of chords (an early form of trigonometry).
III
The Sun's motion and the length of the year.
IV–V
The Moon, and the distances of the Sun and Moon.
VI
Eclipses of the Sun and Moon.
VII–VIII
The fixed stars: a catalog of 1,022 stars in 48 constellations, with positions and brightness on a scale of six magnitudes.
IX–XIII
The five planets: Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter and Saturn.

blocks.html: For each planet Ptolemy used a big circle, the deferent, around the Earth, and a small circle, the epicycle, whose center rides along the deferent. The planet moves on the epicycle. When the planet is on the near side of its epicycle, moving opposite to the epicycle's center, it appears to move backward: retrograde motion.

blocks.name: gb-epicycle
blocks.cap: Change the epicycle's size. With no epicycle there are no loops; at the right size, the picture matches a Sun-centered one exactly.

blocks.html: Ptolemy added two refinements. The Earth is set a little off the center of the deferent (an eccentric). And the epicycle's center moves at a steady angular speed not as seen from the Earth or from the deferent's center but from a third point, the equant, placed on the other side of the center from the Earth. The equant broke the old rule of uniform motion about a circle's center, and many later astronomers disliked it, but it made the predictions much better.

For Mars, Jupiter and Saturn, the line from the epicycle's center to the planet always points the same way as the line from the Earth to the Sun. That is a strong hint that the Sun matters, and it is exactly what a Sun-centered system explains. Copernicus noticed it.

blocks.title: Ptolemy's numbers and the planets' distances
blocks.q: Ptolemy gave Mars an epicycle of radius 39½ on a deferent of radius 60. What is the ratio? Compare it with Earth's distance from the Sun divided by Mars's distance (1 ÷ 1.524).
steps: They agree to within half a percent. Ptolemy's epicycle is, in effect, the Earth's own orbit seen in reverse.

blocks.title: How often does Mars go backward?
blocks.q: Earth goes around the Sun in 1 year, Mars in 1.88 years. How often does Earth overtake Mars, causing a retrograde loop?
steps: Each year Earth gains $1 - \frac{1}{1.88}$ of a lap on Mars.
$1 - 0.532 = 0.468$ of a lap per year.
One full lap takes $1 \div 0.468 \approx 2.14$ years, about 780 days.

blocks.text: Why he kept the Earth still

blocks.html: Ptolemy knew of the idea that the Earth turns. He rejected it with physical arguments: if the Earth spun, clouds and birds and things thrown upward would be left behind toward the west. Answering that objection needed a new physics of motion, which came with Galileo and Newton. Ptolemy was not being stubborn; with the physics of his day, a moving Earth looked impossible.

Believing that by Copernicus's time Ptolemy's system had grown "epicycles on epicycles" to fit the data. The historian Owen Gingerich (1975) showed that the tables in use around 1500 used Ptolemy's original scheme, one epicycle per planet, with no added circles. And Copernicus's own system needed about as many circles as Ptolemy's. The Sun-centered system won because of how it fit together, and later because of Kepler's ellipses, not because it used fewer circles.

blocks.text: What later science kept, and what it changed

items: Kept: the star magnitude scale (modern astronomers still use it, made precise in 1856); much of the trigonometry; the practice of building a model, comparing it with observations and adjusting it.
Changed: the Earth moves (Copernicus, 1543); orbits are ellipses, not circles on circles (Kepler, 1609); all of it follows from gravity (Newton, 1687).

An echo: Kepler's second law makes a planet sweep out equal areas in equal times. Seen from the empty focus of the ellipse, the planet then moves at a nearly steady angular rate, which is just what Ptolemy's equant did.

blocks.html:
🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

Did Ptolemy think his circles were real, or only a way to compute? He seems to have thought both mattered. In the Almagest he aims at models that predict; in a later work, the Planetary Hypotheses, he builds them into a physical system of nested shells and estimates the size of the universe. Medieval astronomers argued about whether astronomy describes the world or only "saves the appearances". The same argument came back when Copernicus's book was published with a preface (not by Copernicus) saying the Sun-centered system was only a calculating device.

Historians also debate how much of Ptolemy's star catalog came from Hipparchus, about 265 years earlier. Most think Ptolemy used and updated Hipparchus's work, as he says he did in places; a few have argued he copied more than he admits.

The Almagest was translated into Arabic in the 800s, and astronomers in Baghdad, Damascus, Maragha and Samarkand checked and improved it. Ibn al-Shatir in Damascus (1300s) replaced the equant with extra small circles in a way very like Copernicus's later models. Gerard of Cremona translated it from Arabic into Latin in 1175. Copernicus learned astronomy from it, and his own book follows its plan.

items: If a theory predicts well but is built on a wrong picture, is it a good theory?
Ptolemy's model worked for 1,400 years. Why might people keep a model that works even when it seems strange?
How would you convince someone that the Earth moves, using only what you can see from your backyard?

blocks.html:
💬 Talk about it together

  1. Act out the Earth and Mars walk. Can you see why Mars seems to go backward?
  2. Ptolemy thought if the Earth spun, things thrown up would land behind us. Why don't they?
  3. Is a good prediction enough, or do we also want a true picture of how things are?
  4. Ptolemy built on Hipparchus, and Copernicus built on Ptolemy. Whose work do you build on when you learn something new?
  5. Look for Mars, Jupiter or Saturn in the night sky (a planet app or almanac can help). Mark its place against the stars over several weeks.
