Owen Gingerich, '"Crisis" versus Aesthetic in the Copernican Revolution', Vistas in Astronomy 17 (1975)

blocks.html: A note for parents: Galen's experiments were done on living animals and he describes them plainly. The lesson tells what he found without detail, and the visual is a simple diagram.

Choose a path

  • 🌱 For young readers
  • 📖 For teens and adults
  • 🔭 Going deeper

🌱 For young readers

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.

Galen was a Greek doctor who lived in the Roman Empire about 1,850 years ago. As a young man he looked after gladiators, the fighters of the Roman games, and later he became doctor to a Roman emperor.

Galen wanted to know how the body does its everyday jobs: how food becomes part of us, how we grow, and how the body gets rid of what it doesn't need. He thought every part of the body has powers (he called them faculties): a power to draw in what it needs, to hold on to it, to change it, and to push out what it doesn't need.
Galen tested his ideas with experiments, which few doctors of his time did. Some of his ideas were later shown to be wrong, but his habit of testing was right.

blocks.name: gb-ureters
blocks.cap: A diagram of Galen's famous test. Tie the tubes from the kidneys and see what happens to the bladder.

blocks.html:
🧩 Try this

Where does the water go? Fold a paper towel into a strip and dip one end into a cup of water. Watch the water climb. A plant does something like this, drawing water up from its roots. Galen thought every part of the body has a power to draw in what it needs. What do you think makes the water climb the paper?

Some people in Galen's day thought the bladder filled up the way a sponge soaks up mist. Galen tied off the tubes that run from the kidneys to the bladder and showed that the bladder stayed empty. Urine is made in the kidneys and flows down those tubes. He was right.

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Galen (AD 129–c. 216) was born in Pergamon, a Greek city in what is now western Turkey. He studied medicine there and in Smyrna and Alexandria, served as physician to the gladiators of Pergamon, and moved to Rome in 162, where he became physician to the emperor Marcus Aurelius and later to his son Commodus. He wrote more than any other ancient author whose works survive, on anatomy, medicine, drugs and philosophy.

On the Natural Faculties takes on one question: how does a living body grow, take in food and get rid of waste? In Galen's day two rival schools gave answers he thought wrong. Followers of Erasistratus explained the body by tubes and pressure, like plumbing. Asclepiades explained it by tiny particles and pores, with nothing directing them. Galen argued that living parts have active powers of their own.

head: Faculty
What it does
Galen's example
rows: Attraction
draws in what is suitable
the kidneys draw urine from the blood
Retention
holds it while it is worked on
the stomach closes around food while digesting it
Alteration
changes it into something new
food changed into blood, blood into flesh
Expulsion
pushes out what is unsuitable or finished
the bladder empties
blocks.cap: The four faculties that serve nutrition, as Galen describes them.

blocks.html: Galen admits he does not know what a faculty is. A faculty is the name for the unknown cause of an observed effect. He is careful about this: he will not claim more knowledge than he has, but he insists that the effects are real and need a cause.

Asclepiades said urine reaches the bladder as vapor, soaking through. Galen answered with an experiment on a living animal. He tied the ureters, the tubes from the kidneys to the bladder. The bladder stayed empty, and the ureters swelled above the ties. When he loosened them, the bladder filled. Urine comes from the kidneys through the ureters, and nowhere else.

blocks.name: gb-ureters
blocks.cap: Tie one or both ureters. The diagram follows what Galen reported.

blocks.html: A good experiment sets two explanations against each other. If urine soaked in as vapor, tying the ureters would change nothing. If it flows down the ureters, the bladder would stay empty. The bladder stayed empty.

Galen uses the magnet as his favorite example: here is something that plainly attracts at a distance, so why deny that a kidney can attract? The comparison is clever. It is also a warning: naming a power is not the same as explaining it, as later scientists who studied magnets (Gilbert, then Faraday, both on this ladder) would show.

Thinking Galen's anatomy is human anatomy. Dissecting human bodies was not done in his Rome, so he dissected animals, especially apes and pigs, and assumed people were built the same. Some of his descriptions are right for apes but wrong for humans. Andreas Vesalius corrected many of them in 1543 from human dissection.

blocks.text: Blood, the liver and the heart

blocks.html: Galen thought food, once digested, went to the liver, which turned it into blood. Blood then spread through the veins and was used up by the body parts as food, so new blood had to be made all the time. Some blood, he thought, passed from the right side of the heart to the left through tiny pores in the wall between them. This picture lasted 1,400 years, until William Harvey (1628, later on this ladder) measured how much blood the heart pumps and showed it must go round and round.

blocks.title: Harvey's kind of estimate
blocks.q: Suppose the heart pushes out 70 mL of blood with each beat and beats 70 times a minute. How much blood is that in an hour? Could the liver make that much from food?
steps: Per minute: $70 \times 70 = 4{,}900$ mL, about 4.9 liters.
Per hour: $4.9 \times 60 = 294$ liters.
That is far more than the food and drink anyone takes in. The same blood must be used again and again.
blocks.a: About 294 liters an hour, so the blood must circulate.

blocks.text: What later medicine kept, and what it changed

items: Kept: experiment on living things, the idea that each organ has its own function (the root of physiology), and the result that the kidneys make urine. Galen also showed, in another book, that arteries carry blood, not air, as Erasistratus had taught.

Changed: the faculties became processes we can explain: filtration in the kidney, muscular movement of the gut, chemical digestion by enzymes. Galen's anatomy was corrected by Vesalius and his blood by Harvey; the four humors were given up in the 1800s.

blocks.html:
🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

Galen believed that nature, which he sometimes calls an artist, does nothing in vain: every part is shaped for its use. He takes this view from Aristotle and Hippocrates. It led him to ask the right question about each organ, what is it for?, and also to accept answers too quickly when an answer seemed fitting. Biologists after Darwin ask the same question in a different way: what did this part do that helped its owners survive and reproduce?

For more than a thousand years, in the Islamic world and in Europe, Galen was "the physician". His books were translated into Syriac, Arabic (by Hunayn ibn Ishaq in the 800s) and Latin. Some later physicians did find errors: Ibn al-Nafis, in Cairo in the 1200s, argued that blood cannot pass through the wall of the heart and must go through the lungs. But most readers took Galen's word over their own eyes. Galen himself had urged doctors to test claims, including old ones. His followers often forgot that part of his teaching.

items: Is it fair to call a power a "faculty" when you don't know what causes it? When does naming help, and when does it hide ignorance?
Galen tested his ideas on animals. People today still argue about when experiments on animals are justified; what do you think the main arguments are on each side?
Why do people go on trusting a famous expert even after some of their claims are shown to be wrong?

blocks.html:
💬 Talk about it together

  1. Galen tested two ideas against each other with one experiment. Can you think of an experiment that would decide between two ideas you have heard?
  2. Galen thought every part of the body has a job. Pick a part of your body and say what you think its job is.
  3. Why might it be hard to correct a famous teacher's mistake, even many years later?
  4. Galen admitted he didn't know what a faculty was. When is it good to say "I don't know"?
  5. Plants and animals both grow and take in food. What can animals do that plants can't, according to Galen?

blocks.html: A note for parents: Augustine is frank that as a young man he lived in ways he later regretted, and that for many years he lived with a woman he did not marry, with whom he had a son. He describes his regrets without detail, and the lesson summarizes them briefly. The Confessions is a Christian book of prayer; the lesson presents Augustine’s beliefs as his own.

Choose a path

  • 🌱 For young readers
  • 📖 For teens and adults
  • 🔭 Going deeper

🌱 For young readers

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.

Augustine grew up in North Africa about 1,650 years ago, in a town that is now in Algeria. He was very clever, and he became a famous teacher of public speaking. His mother, Monica, was a Christian who prayed for him for years. Augustine himself searched for a long time, trying different ideas about God and the world, before he became a Christian too.

Later he wrote the story of his life as a long prayer to God. It is called the Confessions. In it he remembers small things too. Once, when he was sixteen, he and his friends stole pears from a neighbor’s tree. They weren’t even hungry; they threw most of them to pigs. Augustine spent pages asking himself: why did I do it? Just because it was forbidden?

blocks.name: gb-voyage
blocks.cap: Follow Augustine from his home town in Africa to Rome and Milan, and back. Tap Next stop.

blocks.html: In Milan he noticed something surprising: the bishop, Ambrose, read books silently, moving only his eyes. In those days most people read aloud, even alone, so Augustine wrote it down.

🧩 Try this

A memory walk. Augustine wrote that memory is like a huge palace with many rooms. Close your eyes and walk through your home in your mind. In each room, find one memory: a birthday, a game, a meal. Tell the memories to someone in the order of your walk. Did walking through the rooms help you remember?

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Augustine was born in AD 354 in Thagaste, a small town in the Roman province of Africa. His mother Monica was a devout Christian; his father Patricius was not, until near the end of his life. Augustine studied at Carthage, taught rhetoric there, in Rome and then in Milan, where he heard Bishop Ambrose preach. He was baptized at Easter in AD 387, returned to Africa, and in AD 391 the people of Hippo Regius made him a priest. Soon afterward he became their bishop. He wrote the Confessions around AD 397–400, in his forties.
The book is written to God, from beginning to end. The Latin confessio means both confessing one’s faults and praising God. Augustine does both, and invites the reader to listen in.

This sentence is the theme of the whole book: a restless search that finds its rest. Augustine tells his life not as a list of events but as the story of where his heart was looking for rest, and where, in his belief, it finally found it.

head: Books
What happens
rows: I
Infancy and school. He loved Latin stories, and wept for Dido in Virgil, but hated Greek and arithmetic drills.
II
Sixteen: the pear tree. Why do wrong for its own sake?
III–V
Carthage. Cicero’s Hortensius fires him with the love of wisdom. He joins the Manichees for nine years, then grows doubtful and moves to Rome.
VI–VII
Milan. Ambrose’s sermons; the books of the Platonists help him think of God as spiritual and of evil as a lack of good.
VIII
The garden in Milan, AD 386: “Take up and read.”
IX
Baptism; his mother’s death at Ostia.
X
Memory, and who he is now, as he writes.
XI–XIII
Time, eternity and the first chapter of Genesis.

blocks.cap: Augustine’s journeys, from Thagaste to Hippo. Coastlines are simplified.

blocks.html: By AD 386 Augustine believed Christianity was true, he says, but could not bring himself to change his life. Sitting in a garden in Milan with his friend Alypius, he wept.

He opened Paul’s letters and read a verse from Romans 13 urging the reader to leave behind a careless life and “put on the Lord Jesus Christ.” He writes that his doubts vanished. In Latin the children’s words are tolle, lege, now among the most famous words in Christian writing.
The later books turn from his life to great questions. Book XI asks what time is.

The past no longer exists and the future does not yet exist, so how can we measure a long or short time? Augustine’s answer is that we measure time in the mind: memory holds the past, attention the present, and expectation the future. He calls time a “stretching” of the mind (distentio animi). God, he holds, is not in time at all but in an eternal present.

Reading the Confessions as a modern memoir. Augustine leaves out most of what a biographer would want (his son’s mother is never named) and dwells on moments that show his inner search. And the last four books are not a life story at all, but reflections on memory, time and creation.

items: Autobiography: the Confessions is often called the first great autobiography in the West: a person looking with open eyes at his own inner life.
Philosophy: his questions about time and memory are still discussed by philosophers and psychologists.
Christian thought: for Christians of many traditions, it has been a classic of prayer and of the story of conversion for 1,600 years.

blocks.html:
🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

Augustine grew up in a Roman Empire that had recently become Christian under Constantine, while many people, including much of the educated class, still followed the old religions. He moved between them: a pagan education in Virgil and Cicero, the Manichee sect, Platonist philosophy, and finally the Catholic Church of Ambrose. The Confessions records how he weighed each of these; it is his own account and judgment of them.

items: Why do people sometimes do wrong just because it is forbidden, like the pear theft?
What is time? Can you explain it to someone without using a clock?
Is your memory a part of who you are? If you forgot everything, would you still be you?
Can a person know what is right and still not be able to do it? What finally helps?

blocks.html: Augustine’s next great work, the City of God, turned from one soul’s story to the story of all humanity. Petrarch, a thousand years later, carried a copy of the Confessions and said he opened it at random on a mountaintop, as Augustine had opened Paul. Rousseau, later on this ladder, wrote his own Confessions in the 18th century, but as a defense of himself before other people rather than a prayer.

💬 Talk about it together

  1. Augustine stole pears he did not even want. Have you ever done something just because it was not allowed? Why do you think people do that?
  2. Monica prayed for her son for many years. What does it mean to keep caring about someone who is going the wrong way?
  3. “If no one asks me, I know: if I wish to explain it, I know not.” What else is like that, easy to use but hard to explain?
  4. Augustine noticed Ambrose reading silently. What small thing have you noticed about someone that surprised you?
  5. Why might someone write their life story as a letter or prayer, rather than a report?

blocks.html: A note for parents: The City of God is a work of Christian theology and of argument against the Roman religion of its day. The lesson presents Augustine’s beliefs and arguments as his own, and notes where readers have disagreed. It mentions the sack of Rome and other wars without detail.

🌱 For young readers

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.

In AD 410 an army of Goths broke into the city of Rome and looted it for three days. Rome had not been captured by an enemy in 800 years. People all over the empire were shocked. Some said: this happened because Rome stopped worshiping the old gods and became Christian.

Augustine, a bishop in North Africa, wrote a huge book to answer them. He called it the City of God. He said that there are really two “cities” in the world, two kinds of people mixed together everywhere. They are not two places on a map. One is made of people who love themselves most of all. The other is made of people who love God most of all, and their neighbors as themselves. Augustine believed that earthly cities, even Rome, rise and fall, but that the city of God would last forever.

blocks.name: gb-two-cities
blocks.cap: Augustine’s two cities, running side by side through the ages of history. Tap an age.

blocks.html:
🧩 Try this

Two kinds of towns. Draw two small towns side by side. In the first, everyone does whatever is best for themselves. In the second, everyone thinks first of others. Draw what the playground, the shops and the roads look like in each. Then talk: which town would you want to live in? Which one is more like the real world, or is ours a mix, as Augustine thought?

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Augustine (AD 354–430) had been bishop of Hippo, in North Africa, for about fifteen years when the Visigoths under Alaric sacked Rome in August 410. Refugees reached Africa with their stories, and with a charge: Rome’s gods had protected it for a thousand years, and now that the empire had turned to Christianity they had abandoned it. Encouraged by his friend Marcellinus, an imperial official sent to Africa, Augustine began the City of God in 413 and finished it in 426, four years before he died.

head: Books
What Augustine argues
rows: I–V
The old gods did not give Rome its earthly success, and disasters struck Rome long before Christianity.
VI–X
Nor can they give happiness after death. Here he engages the best pagan thinkers, especially the Platonists, with respect and with disagreement.
XI–XIV
The beginnings of the two cities: creation, the angels, the first human beings.
XV–XVIII
Their course through history, from Cain and Abel to his own time.
XIX–XXII
Their ends: peace, judgment, and the eternal city.

blocks.html: The two cities are defined by what people love most, not by where they live. In this life they are mixed together: the city of God is a pilgrim, a traveler passing through, living among the earthly city and using its peace. Augustine does not simply equal one city with the Church and the other with the Roman state; he says the true membership of each will be known only at the end.

blocks.cap: The ages of history as Augustine counts them in Book XXII. Tap an age to see what he discusses there.

blocks.html: One of Augustine’s sharpest pages asks what makes a government different from a gang.
The pirate story was older; Augustine found it in Cicero. His point is that size and success do not make a state just. What makes a government more than a band of robbers is justice.

In Book XIX Augustine argues that everyone, even people at war, wants peace of some kind, and defines it in a phrase that became famous: peace is “the tranquillity of order” (tranquillitas ordinis), each thing in its proper place. Earthly peace is good and both cities use it, he says, but it is always partial and fragile. Only the city of God, in his belief, will know perfect peace.

Reading the book as a plan for a Christian government. Augustine is not drawing up a constitution. He is arguing that no earthly state, Christian or not, should be mistaken for the city of God, and that Christians should be good citizens of the earthly city while not putting their final hope in it. Later readers have drawn very different political conclusions from the book.

items: A philosophy of history: Augustine read all of history as one story with a direction and an end, instead of endless cycles. That idea shaped Western thinking about history for centuries.

Church and state: medieval writers argued over his two cities when they debated the powers of popes and kings. His biographer Einhard says Charlemagne liked to have the City of God read to him at dinner.
Politics without illusions: modern thinkers of many kinds still cite his view that states are needed to keep a limited peace, but are never perfect.

blocks.html:
🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

blocks.text: Context: the end of an age

blocks.html: The Western Roman Empire was weakening. Augustine died in 430 while the Vandals were besieging his own city of Hippo. Some later readers have seen the City of God as the farewell of the ancient world and the first great book of the Middle Ages. It argues with Roman history, Varro’s writings on the gods, Cicero’s Republic and the Platonists, and so preserves much of what they said.

items: What do you love most? Augustine thought that answer shows which “city” a person belongs to. Is he right that what we love shapes who we are?
What makes a government different from a gang of robbers?
Can a country be good if it does not last? Can it be great if it is not just?
Is peace just the absence of war, or something more?

blocks.html: Thomas Aquinas, in the next era, drew on Augustine while giving more room to natural reason in political life. Dante pictured the eternal city in his Paradiso. Machiavelli, later on this ladder, asked what rulers must do to keep a state in a world where people are not good, a very different starting point. Gibbon, in the 18th century, blamed Christianity in part for Rome’s fall, reviving the very charge Augustine answered; historians since have weighed many other causes.

💬 Talk about it together

  1. Augustine says two cities are made by two loves: love of self and love of God. What would a town look like if everyone in it loved others as themselves?
  2. What is the difference between a king and a pirate, according to the pirate? Do you agree?
  3. Why might people look for someone to blame after a disaster? Is that fair?
  4. Augustine called peace “the tranquillity of order.” What would that mean in your home or classroom?
  5. Can something be great without being good?

blocks.html: A note for parents: On Christian Doctrine is a guide to reading and teaching the Bible, written by a Christian bishop for Christian teachers. The lesson presents Augustine’s aims and rules as his own, and draws out the parts about signs, language and speaking that any reader can use.

  • 📖 For teens and adults

🌱 For young readers

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.

Augustine was a bishop in North Africa who had once been a teacher of public speaking. He wrote a book for people who read the Bible and teach it to others. It is called On Christian Doctrine; “doctrine” here means teaching.

Augustine noticed that everything we learn comes to us through signs. A sign is something that makes you think of something else. Some signs happen by themselves: when you see smoke, you think of fire, even though nobody sent the smoke as a message. Augustine called these natural signs. Other signs are given on purpose, like words, a nod or a wave. He called these conventional signs, because people agree on what they mean.

blocks.name: gb-signs
blocks.cap: Is it a plain thing, a natural sign or a given sign? Choose, then tap Next example.

blocks.html:
🧩 Try this

A sign hunt. Walk around your home or street and find five natural signs (wet pavement means it rained; a wagging tail means a happy dog) and five given signs (a stop sign, a label, a clock face, a smile meant for you). Make two lists. Which list was easier? Can you find something that could be both?

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Augustine (AD 354–430) began On Christian Doctrine (Latin De doctrina christiana) soon after he became bishop of Hippo, around AD 396. He stopped partway through the third book and came back to it about thirty years later, in 426–427, when he finished Book III and added Book IV. His purpose was practical: to teach Christian readers how to understand the Bible, and preachers how to explain it to others. Along the way he wrote one of the first careful accounts of how signs and language work.

Book I is about things. Augustine divides them into things to be enjoyed, loved for their own sake, and things to be used, loved for the sake of something else (in Latin, frui and uti). In his view only God is to be enjoyed in the full sense, and everything else rightly loved in relation to God. The whole aim of Scripture, he says, is love of God and of neighbor: whoever thinks he understands the Bible but does not build up that double love has not yet understood it.

Natural signs point to something without anyone intending them to: smoke, a footprint, an angry face. Conventional (given) signs are used on purpose to pass a thought from one mind to another: words above all, and also nods, gestures, flags and trumpet calls. Written letters are signs of spoken words, so writing is a sign of a sign.

blocks.name: gb-signs
blocks.cap: Sort Augustine’s examples, and some of ours, into things, natural signs and conventional signs.

blocks.text: Hard passages and the tools to read them

blocks.html: Book II asks why Scripture is sometimes hard to understand. Signs can be unknown (you do not know the word or the thing it names) or ambiguous (they could mean more than one thing). For unknown signs, Augustine says, learn the languages, Hebrew and Greek, and compare translations; learn history, natural history, numbers and music. He argues that a Christian should take whatever is true and useful in pagan learning, as the Israelites carried gold and silver out of Egypt, and he puts the principle simply:

Book III takes up ambiguous signs, and especially the question of when to read words literally and when figuratively. One of his rules: a passage that, read literally, would seem to recommend something contrary to love or to good morals should be read as figurative. He also discusses the seven rules of interpretation of an earlier African writer, Tyconius.

blocks.text: Book IV: to teach, to delight, to persuade

blocks.html: The former professor of rhetoric now writes about speaking. He borrows Cicero’s three aims of the speaker.

Teaching comes first: a speaker who is not understood, Augustine says, has not yet said anything to his hearer. He matches Cicero’s three styles to the three aims: the subdued (plain) style for teaching, the temperate (middle) style for delighting, and the majestic (grand) style for moving people to act. A good speaker mixes them, and his life must match his words, or his words will carry little weight.

Thinking Augustine rejects rhetoric because it is pagan. He says rhetoric is a tool that can serve truth or falsehood, so those who teach truth should not leave it to those who teach lies. What he warns against is eloquence without wisdom: a beautiful speech that says nothing true.

items: Education: for the whole Middle Ages this book was a charter for Christian learning, justifying the study of grammar, rhetoric, history and the sciences.
The study of signs: Augustine’s definition of a sign and his split between natural and conventional signs are still discussed by philosophers of language.
Preaching and speaking: Book IV is often called the first Christian handbook of rhetoric, and teachers of speech still use its three aims.

blocks.html:
🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

blocks.text: Context: a teacher of speech becomes a bishop

blocks.html: Augustine had spent his early career teaching young men to speak persuasively in court and in public. As a bishop he preached often to ordinary people in a busy port city. This book brings the two lives together. It also reflects a real question in the Church of his time: should Christians study the pagan classics, Virgil and Cicero, or leave them alone? Augustine’s answer, keep what is true and useful, shaped Christian schools for a thousand years.

items: Is everything we learn really learned through signs? What about learning to ride a bike?
Can a beautiful speech be bad? Can a plain one be great?
How should we decide whether words are meant literally or as a figure of speech?
Should a speaker try to delight and persuade, or only to teach?

blocks.html: Thomas Aquinas, in the next era, discusses the literal and spiritual senses of Scripture, building on Augustine. Erasmus, in the Renaissance, renewed the call to read Scripture in Hebrew and Greek. Much later, Locke’s Essay Concerning Human Understanding, on this ladder, opened a new study of words as signs of ideas.

💬 Talk about it together

  1. What signs have you used today without words? (A nod, a wave, a thumbs-up.)
  2. Augustine says a speaker who is not understood has said nothing. Have you ever explained something and not been understood? What did you change?
  3. Which matters most in a speech: teaching, delighting, or persuading? Why?
  4. “Wherever truth may be found, it belongs to his Master.” Why might Augustine want Christians to study books by people who did not share their faith?
  5. Can you think of a sentence that means something different when read literally and when read as a figure of speech?
